\chapter{Family}
\label{ch:it-family}
\hlchaptermodality{10}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name my parents and my siblings in Italian and spot the little-ending Italian bolted onto frater and soror.}

Say il padre, la madre, il fratello, la sorella, then rebuild fratello from frāter plus the diminutive -ello and reach English fraternal and sorority from the same roots.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[il padre, la madre]{il padre, la madre — closest to Latin}

\label{lesson:IT-C10-genitori}



\begin{quote}
Italian, as ever, stays nearest to Rome. Its \textbf{padre} (\textquotedblleft{}father\textquotedblright{}) and \textbf{madre} (\textquotedblleft{}mother\textquotedblright{}) barely moved from Latin \textbf{pater} and \textbf{māter} — Latin just softened the \emph{-t-} to \emph{-d-}. If you know the Latin, you nearly know the Italian.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{il padre} (\textquotedblleft{}father\textquotedblright{}) $\leftarrow$ Latin \textbf{pater} (\emph{-t- $\to$ -d-}).
  \item \textbf{la madre} (\textquotedblleft{}mother\textquotedblright{}) $\leftarrow$ Latin \textbf{māter} (\emph{-t- $\to$ -d-}).
\end{itemize}

Articles: \emph{il} padre (masculine), \emph{la} madre (feminine).

\textbf{English already borrowed one of these whole:} a \textbf{padre} is what English (and Spanish-influenced) speakers call a priest or military chaplain — \emph{padre} itself, untouched.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{cousinweb}
Italian \textquotedblleft{}parents\textquotedblright{} is \textbf{i genitori} — not from \emph{parens} but from Latin \textbf{genitor}, \textquotedblleft{}the \textbf{begetter},\textquotedblright{} from \emph{gignere} \textquotedblleft{}to beget/bring forth.\textquotedblright{} That root \emph{gen-} \textquotedblleft{}give birth to\textquotedblright{} is everywhere in English: \textbf{genital, progenitor, genesis, generate, genus, gene}. So \emph{i genitori} are literally \textquotedblleft{}the begetters.\textquotedblright{} (Beware the \textbf{false friend}: Italian \emph{parenti} means \textbf{relatives} in general, \emph{not} \textquotedblleft{}parents\textquotedblright{}!)

The Latin-through-English adjectives still come from \emph{pater/māter}: \textbf{paternal} and \textbf{maternal} — the same roots as French \emph{père/mère} and, by Grimm's law, English \emph{father/mother}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}il padre, la madre\textquotedblright{} — soft \emph{-d-} where Latin had \emph{-t-}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}i genitori = the parents; \emph{genitor} = begetter $\to$ genesis, gene\textquotedblright{}
  \item the false-friend warning — \textquotedblleft{}\emph{parenti} = relatives, NOT parents\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give \textquotedblleft{}father\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}mother\textquotedblright{} with articles. (\textbf{il padre, la madre}.) What single sound did Latin \emph{pater/māter} soften to? (The \emph{-t-} became \textbf{-d-}.) What does \textbf{genitori} literally mean, and name an English cousin. (\textquotedblleft{}The \textbf{begetters}\textquotedblright{}; genesis/gene/progenitor.) What does the false friend \emph{parenti} mean? (\textbf{Relatives}, not parents.) Next: \textbf{fratello} and \textbf{sorella}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[il fratello, la sorella]{il fratello, la sorella — brother and sister, with a little-ending}

\label{lesson:IT-C10-fratello-sorella}



\begin{quote}
Here Italian does something charming. Where French kept \emph{frère} and \emph{sœur} bare, Italian rebuilt \textquotedblleft{}brother\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}sister\textquotedblright{} with its beloved \textbf{diminutive} endings — literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{little brother}\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{little sister}\textquotedblright{} — and those forms became the everyday words.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{il fratello} (\textquotedblleft{}brother\textquotedblright{}) $\leftarrow$ Latin \textbf{frāter} + the diminutive \textbf{-ellus} $\to$ \emph{fraterellus} $\to$ \emph{fratello}, once \textquotedblleft{}little brother.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textbf{la sorella} (\textquotedblleft{}sister\textquotedblright{}) $\leftarrow$ Latin \textbf{soror} + the diminutive \textbf{-ella} $\to$ \emph{sorella}, once \textquotedblleft{}little sister.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

The root still shows: \textbf{frat-} and \textbf{soror-}, the same roots English turns into \textbf{frat}ernal, \textbf{frat}ernity, \textbf{friar} and \textbf{soror}ity, \textbf{soror}al. Italian just wrapped them in the affectionate \emph{-ello/-ella} that also gives \emph{fratello}'s cousins across the language (\emph{-ello} on \emph{poverello} \textquotedblleft{}poor little one,\textquotedblright{} \emph{-ella} on countless names).
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item all four — \textquotedblleft{}il padre, la madre, il fratello, la sorella\textquotedblright{}
  \item the build — \textquotedblleft{}\emph{frater} + \emph{-ello} $\to$ fratello, 'little brother'\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}fratello $\to$ fraternal; sorella $\to$ sorority\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give \textquotedblleft{}brother\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}sister\textquotedblright{} with articles. (\textbf{il fratello, la sorella}.) What did Italian \textbf{add} to Latin \emph{frāter/soror} to make them? (A \textbf{diminutive} ending, \emph{-ello / -ella} — \textquotedblleft{}little brother/sister.\textquotedblright{}) Name an English cousin of each root. (\emph{frat-} $\to$ fraternal/friar; \emph{soror-} $\to$ sorority.) Next chapter: sentences about the family.
\end{tcolorbox}
